howIWorkSection.title: Four principles behind every decision
howIWorkSection.description: Four principles for the architecture and system decisions I make on every project.

principles.title: Build for real users.
principles.detail: I design around how people actually behave, not how systems assume they should.

principles.title: Modernize before rewriting.
principles.detail: I evolve systems incrementally with parity checks instead of betting on a full rewrite, because full rewrites often fail under the exact production pressure they were meant to solve.

principles.title: Measure before optimizing.
principles.detail: I base optimization work on real usage data and clear baselines, not assumptions.

principles.title: Leave systems easier to maintain.
principles.detail: Each change should reduce complexity so the next engineer can extend the system without friction.

items.title: Build for people who depend on it
items.description: Slow pages and brittle interfaces fail before the task does.
items.details: I care about load time, clear interfaces, and behavior on the devices people actually use. Whether it's healthcare, civic platforms, or education, the goal is the same: help someone finish what they came to do.

items.title: Keep it simple at scale
items.description: Choose the simplest design that still works as the system grows.
items.details: I've seen petition traffic spike overnight and watched MongoDB queries go from milliseconds to seconds. I think about scale, latency, and maintenance early, then propose the simplest design that still meets the need.

items.title: Code others can maintain
items.description: Readable software lasts longer than clever software.
items.details: Easy to read code, sensible architecture, and reliable releases. I prefer understanding HTML, HTTP, and data storage before reaching for another library. Fast delivery matters, but so does leaving behind software the next developer can trust.

items.title: Clear with the team
items.description: Say what you mean. Leave enough context for later.
items.details: I pair, review code, and plan with designers, product managers, and backend engineers. I document decisions, explain trade-offs in plain language, and make it clear why a choice was made, not just what shipped.

backgroundHook: I'm **Ansumana Darboe**. Most people call me **Ansu**. I'm a Senior Software Engineer based in **Berlin**, and for the past 8+ years I've been building web and mobile software people actually have to rely on.
The curiosity started with our family computer. I was the kid who took things apart to see what was inside. These days I do the same with large codebases. Fewer missing screws. More late nights.

Before tech, I spent over four years playing professional football and coaching youth teams in **The Gambia**. Our coach had one phrase after any session he considered poor. 'Again tomorrow.' That was it. He picked up his bag and walked off the pitch. I never liked hearing it. I understand it better now.

A knee injury ended the football chapter. I taught in rural classrooms with cracked blackboards and few textbooks. I studied Software Applications at **Gambia Technical Training Institute**, managed networks at **AccounTax Solutions**, and moved to **Berlin** in 2014 without speaking the language or knowing anyone. I believed if I could learn code, I could learn German too.

Since then the work has taken me through very different worlds. I rebuilt the React Native app for real estate teams at **Propstack** and worked on civic platforms at **change.org** and **innn.it**, where a slow page wasn't just an inconvenience. It affected how quickly people could discover, support, and share campaigns. Later I co-founded **ZULA**, a storytelling platform for children who rarely saw themselves reflected in the books they read. I joined **FREY ADV** to lead the frontend rebuild of a practice management system that had run on desktops for over thirty years, and after Frey acquired **doctorly** I moved onto that team. Since mid-2026 I've held the frontend lead rotation there: setting the quarter's priorities, writing the architecture decisions behind them, and mentoring the engineers shipping beside me.

Most days you'll find me working with **TypeScript**, **React**, **Node.js**, and cloud infrastructure. I enjoy improving performance, simplifying complex systems, mentoring junior developers, and building software that quietly does its job. The stack changes. Building software people can rely on doesn't.
Outside of work I still follow football closely. These days my knee prefers that I watch more matches than I play.

growth.title: One real misjudgement, and what changed
growth.description: Not a philosophy. One real misjudgement, what it cost, and what changed.
paragraphs: When I moved onto a new team, I was asked directly whether I knew test-driven development. I said no. They handed me the testing lead for a new module anyway.

I also shipped merge requests that were too large to review properly, and once pushed a change straight to the main branch instead of opening a request for it. Both slowed the team down, including me. Reviewers had to hold a week of changes in their heads at once, and a direct push meant nobody had checked the change before it shipped.

I broke the work into smaller pieces and started taking testing seriously instead of treating it as a step to get through. Within a few months I was writing tests that described what a user does, not just what the code does internally, so they would survive me changing the implementation later.

By the middle of that year I was leading the same kind of testing work I had said no to months earlier, and soon after took on the frontend lead rotation for the team. I would rather admit that arc than polish it away.

items.title: doctorly
items.summary: Frontend lead for a clinical practice platform used by 1,000+ medical staff: sequencing priorities, writing the architecture decisions, and handing ownership to the team as it grows.
items.description: After FREY ADV acquired doctorly, I moved onto the team building its clinical practice platform. Since mid-2026 I've held the frontend lead rotation: setting the quarter's priorities, authoring the architecture decisions behind them, and delegating ownership of individual streams as the team grows.
achievements: Consolidated state management to one story: server state in React Query, shared client state in Zustand, and removed the last Redux usage from the platform.
Authored the frontend observability decision record, covering tool choice, PII scrubbing, and release and source-map strategy, and held implementation until sign-off.

Split the observability build into separate merge requests for bootstrap, PII scrubbing, technical context, error capture and failure behaviour, so privacy and failure handling could be reviewed on their own.

Reviewed the team's merge requests with feedback aimed at behaviour rather than style: a request firing on every keystroke where comparable flows debounce, an unreachable fallback branch, a dropped error notification because a refetch does not reject by default.
items.problem: doctorly's interface had been built for desktop screens only, with no responsive layout for the tablets and phones clinicians increasingly used. After Frey acquired the company, the team needed frontend direction: which of the quarter's priorities actually mattered, how to migrate domain-by-domain without freezing delivery, and how to make production errors actionable instead of merely logged.
solution: Sequenced the quarter's frontend priorities instead of running them in parallel. Architecture boundaries, the data layer, observability and multi-tenancy each constrained the next, so the order mattered more than the count.

Consolidated state management to one story: server state in React Query, shared client state in Zustand, and local state where it belongs. Removed the last Redux usage from the platform in the process.
Ran a domain-by-domain consolidation as a series of small merge requests, deleting each legacy path in the same change that replaced it, so the moves stayed reviewable.
Authored the frontend observability decision record and held implementation until sign-off, because the PII scrubbing and release handling were the parts worth not redoing.
Held an urgent piece of work in the backlog because it depended on a backend decision about how a tenant is identified, rather than inventing a frontend-only answer that would need unpicking later.

technicalInsights.title: Sequencing, Not Parallel Migrations
technicalInsights.description: The quarter's priorities were not independent projects. Architecture boundaries, data ownership, observability and multi-tenancy each affected the others. Trade-off: some work stayed visibly unstarted, and the work that did start got finished.

technicalInsights.title: Documentation as Tooling, Not a File
technicalInsights.description: Wrote the frontend rules into the tooling engineers use during implementation and review. Trade-off: more setup cost upfront, but the guidance surfaces exactly when decisions get made instead of sitting unread.

technicalInsights.title: Deferring a Decision Deliberately
technicalInsights.description: Held an urgent tenant-identification feature in the backlog pending a backend decision. Trade-off: the work stayed visibly unstarted, but a frontend-only answer would have needed unpicking once the backend direction landed.

outcome.impact: The team ships fewer, better-sequenced changes, and a production error now carries enough context to act on without redoing the investigation each time.
businessResults: 1,000+ medical staff use the rebuilt platform.
Redux is gone from the platform: server state in React Query, shared client state in Zustand, local state in the component.
Consolidating the LDT and Practice areas removed roughly 1,100 lines of duplicate implementation.

lessonsLearned: Choosing not to ship something urgent, and being able to say why, is harder than shipping it.
Splitting a migration into reviewable merge requests costs more upfront planning than one big change, and saves the multi-week review nobody wants to do.

What I got wrong: I once assumed a piece of backend work was already finished and shipped my side of a feature flag change without looping in QA or a backend engineer first. It caused a rollout hiccup that ten minutes of coordination would have caught.
technicalChallengesOvercome: Ordered a quarter of connected frontend priorities so each one made the next safer to start.
Migrated legacy state management domain-by-domain while keeping every intermediate step shippable.
Made production errors actionable by attaching route, environment, and release context without exposing patient data.

items.title: Quincy Mobile
items.summary: A 30+ year practice management stack, rebuilt for clinicians who need speed, secure remote access, and software that works when ward WiFi does not.
items.description: The old desktop system kept staff tied to one room. We rebuilt it as a responsive web and mobile platform in React and TypeScript. The work is speed, reliability, and workflows that match how medical teams actually move through a day.
achievements: Built frontend features for the responsive rebuild of a practice management system that had run on desktops for over thirty years: patient, appointment and document workflows in React and TypeScript.
Redesigned patient, appointment, and document workflows with clinicians in the room, not from a whiteboard alone.
Implemented secure authentication, encryption, and role-based access from day one rather than bolting security on after launch.
Paired and reviewed across the codebase, mostly on behaviour, edge cases, and how changes fit the patterns already there.
items.problem: Legacy desktop software locked clinicians to one room, added minutes to every workflow, and made remote access a security afterthought. The constraint: modernize without disrupting daily operations in a regulated environment.
solution: Chose a modular React + TypeScript frontend over a full rewrite in a new framework, so teams could ship UI improvements incrementally while legacy services stayed stable.
Extracted shared UI primitives, the peek drawer, composer shell and responsive hooks, once the same patterns turned up in a third feature, instead of letting each screen grow its own.
Adopted mobile-responsive, offline-first patterns where connectivity was unreliable, accepting higher sync complexity to avoid blocking patient-facing workflows.
Integrated role-based access with GDPR-aligned encryption rather than bolting security on after launch.
Established automated testing and CI/CD so frequent releases did not require weekend deploy windows.

technicalInsights.title: Shared Primitives Over Per-Screen Copies
technicalInsights.description: Pulled the peek drawer, composer shell and responsive hooks into shared pieces. Trade-off: more coordination when a primitive changes, less duplicate behaviour to fix in five places.

technicalInsights.title: Security-First Design
technicalInsights.description: Multi-layer auth and encryption from day one. Rejected a faster 'auth later' path because healthcare incidents are harder to unwind than slower initial delivery.

technicalInsights.title: Offline-Ready Experience
technicalInsights.description: Service workers and local caching for intermittent hospital networks. Accepted conflict-resolution edge cases rather than forcing online-only flows that failed in production.

outcome.impact: Clinicians can work from more places without fighting slow software or insecure access. Patient care moves a little faster when the tools keep up.
businessResults: Patient-list and appointment routes loaded noticeably faster after code splitting and caching.
Secure remote access for 1,000+ medical staff.
Complaints about slow or confusing software dropped after clinician-led redesigns.

lessonsLearned: Clinicians will tell you what is broken if you sit in the room long enough.
Security and usability are not opposites in healthcare. They fail together when either is ignored.

What I got wrong: I first resolved offline sync conflicts by keeping whichever version synced last and treated it as a rare edge case. A nurse found a case where an earlier, legitimate update got silently overwritten. We rebuilt sync to flag the conflict for a person to resolve instead, even though it made syncing slower.
technicalChallengesOvercome: Migrated legacy data and workflows to a modern React architecture without disrupting daily operations.
Built a secure, fast login system usable by busy clinicians.
Ensured consistent, reliable performance across variable hospital and remote network conditions.
technicalChallenges: Maintaining real-time data sync across multiple devices and users.
Supporting offline use without silently losing data on conflict.
Scaling role-based permissions for complex, evolving clinical workflows.

solution: Chose a modular Node.js + React stack on AWS over a managed BaaS. More setup, but predictable cost and control at 5,000+ users.
Prioritized offline-first mobile UX with service workers instead of online-only React SPA patterns that failed in the field.
Automated Docker/Kubernetes deploys early, accepting pipeline complexity during rapid iteration in exchange for materially faster releases.
Added a no-code CMS so non-technical contributors could publish, trading engineering purity for content velocity.
Tuned caching and Lambda/S3 allocation monthly; rejected over-provisioned instances that looked safe on paper but drained runway.

technicalInsights.title: Cloud-Native Flexibility
technicalInsights.description: AWS Lambda, S3, and Docker for scale-to-zero workloads. Trade-off: cold starts and observability setup versus fixed servers we could not afford at early stage.

technicalInsights.title: Offline-First UX
technicalInsights.description: Service workers and local storage for interrupted connections. Accepted sync conflict handling rather than blocking reads when networks dropped mid-session.

technicalInsights.title: No-Code Content

items.title: Event-Driven Microservices: When Your App Gets Too Big
items.summary: There was a time deploy took thirty seconds. Then the codebase grew, teams multiplied, and nobody wanted to touch production on a Friday. This is how I split a monolith into services that talk through events, with Node.js, Docker, and Kubernetes.

sections.content: Event-Driven Microservices: When Your App Gets Too Big

There was a time deploy took thirty seconds. Then the codebase grew, teams multiplied, and Friday releases became something you avoided. The monolith still worked, mostly. Nobody wanted to be the person who broke it.

Microservices split that pressure into smaller services, each with one job. A user service handles auth. A notification service sends email. When one fails, the others keep running. The tradeoff is more moving parts to watch.

Event-driven architecture is one way to keep those services from tangling. Instead of calling each other directly, they communicate through events. A service announces that something happened. Every other service decides whether that event matters to them.
1. Why Microservices Matter
Fixing a footer typo used to mean deploying the entire application. One database outage could take everything offline. Smaller services limit the blast radius.
Each service does one thing. If payments break, login still works. If email stalls, orders still process. Independence is the point. It is also the cost.
2. How Services Talk to Each Other

When a user signs up, the user service saves the record and publishes UserCreated. Email sends welcome mail. Analytics records the signup. Each listener handles its own failure without blocking the request.
The user service does not need to know who is listening. Publishing an event should feel like dropping a letter into a mailbox. Once it is sent, your work is finished.
Name events after facts, not commands. UserCreated is better than SendWelcomeEmail. Facts age well. Commands get argued about in code review forever.

Events are not a religion. If you need an immediate answer before you can continue, a direct request is fine. A useful rule: if failure in step three should not roll back step one, step three probably should not be inline.
3. Let's Build Something Real

Enough theory. Here is a simple user system: a React frontend, a Node.js backend, Redis Pub/Sub for events, MongoDB for persistence, Docker for local consistency, and Kubernetes for production orchestration.

mkdir event-driven-microservice
cd event-driven-microservice
npm init -y

Keep the layout simple and domain-focused. Use kebab-case for files, colocate related code, put constants and types in their own files, and keep components thin. Business logic belongs in hooks and utilities, not scattered across JSX.

└── kubernetes/
    ├── frontend-deployment.yaml
    └── backend-deployment.yaml
4. Building the Frontend: Keep It Simple
The frontend collects user data and posts it to the backend. It does not send email, update analytics, or notify a CRM. That belongs elsewhere.

npx create-react-app frontend
cd frontend
npm install axios
Shared Types First
Define request and response shapes once. Avoid any. TypeScript should catch contract drift before runtime does.
API Helper: Your Communication Bridge
Centralize HTTP calls in one helper. Read the API URL from the environment so local, Docker, and production stay configurable.
Form Logic in a Hook
Keep the component focused on rendering. Form state, validation, and submit handling live in a custom hook.
The Form Component: Presentation Only
Semantic HTML, labels, and keyboard-friendly controls. The component renders state; it does not own the workflow.
5. Building the Backend: The Brain of Your System
Do not start with routes. Start with responsibilities: validate, persist, publish. Keep route handlers small. Push validation and event wiring into utilities you can test without HTTP.

cd backend
npm init -y
npm install express mongoose redis @godaddy/terminus
npm install -D typescript @types/express @types/node ts-node
Constants and Event Types
Validation Utility
Pure validation functions are easy to test and reuse. Return a message or null instead of throwing inside the validator.
Database Connection: Don't Skip This
Error Handler Middleware
One consistent error response shape beats try/catch copy-pasted in every route.
Server Startup
The Main Server
User Model
This tutorial stores a plain password to stay small. In production, hash with bcrypt or argon2 before save and never return password fields in API responses.
The API Route
Validate. Save. Publish. Return only safe fields. That is the whole handler.
Events: The Heart of Microservices
Publishers and subscribers stay in one module, but channel names live in constants. Redis Pub/Sub is fine for learning. Kafka or RabbitMQ enter the picture when you need durable replay.
A separate consumer might send welcome email or record analytics. Each can fail independently. Each can be tested with a fake event without booting the whole platform.
6. Docker: Making Deployment Easy
Docker's biggest win is often consistency, not portability alone. My machine works stops being a category of bug when everyone runs the same containers.

# frontend/Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

# backend/Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3001
CMD ["npm", "start"]
docker-compose: Run Everything Locally

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      REACT_APP_API_URL: http://localhost:3001/api
    depends_on:
      - backend
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "3001:3001"
    environment:
      DB_URL: mongodb://mongo:27017/app
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      PORT: 3001
    depends_on:
      - mongo
      - redis
  mongo:
    image: mongo:7
  redis:
    image: redis:7
docker compose up --build
7. Kubernetes: Managing Your Services at Scale
Running one container is easy. Running many is not. Kubernetes schedules containers, restarts failed pods, and scales replicas. You declare desired state; the cluster enforces it.

# kubernetes/frontend-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: frontend
          image: frontend:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: frontend-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: frontend
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3000
      targetPort: 3000

# kubernetes/backend-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: backend
          image: backend:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3001
          env:
            - name: DB_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: app-secrets
                  key: db-url
            - name: REDIS_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: app-secrets
                  key: redis-url
            - name: PORT
              value: "3001"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: backend
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3001
      targetPort: 3001

kubectl apply -f kubernetes/frontend-deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f kubernetes/backend-deployment.yaml
8. What You Should Know Before Going Live
Microservices are not free. They solve some problems and introduce others. Know both sides before you split a monolith.
The Good Stuff

items: Independent deployments: fix one service without breaking others
Team autonomy: different teams can own different services
Fault isolation: one service failure does not kill everything
Scaling flexibility: scale only what needs scaling
Loose coupling through events: add consumers without touching the publisher
Thin components and typed contracts: easier to read, test, and change

sections.content: The Reality Check

items: More complexity: you are managing multiple services instead of one
Network failures: services talking over the network can fail in new ways
Data consistency: keeping state in sync across services is hard
Debugging across boundaries: centralized logs and tracing become essential
Operational overhead: more moving parts means more things to monitor
Events can arrive twice: design consumers to be idempotent
Events can arrive out of order: never assume timing unless you design for it
Security basics matter: hash passwords, hide secrets, validate every input

sections.content: What's Next?
You have a minimal event-driven setup. Extend it with auth, structured logging, monitoring, tests, and a durable broker if replay matters.

items: Hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2 before persistence
Add authentication and authorization
Implement structured logging and a shared error response format
Set up metrics, traces, and alerting
Write unit tests for validators, publishers, and consumers
Swap Redis for Kafka or RabbitMQ if you need durable replay
Add circuit breakers when calls cross the network

sections.content: Start with a monolith until pain is real. Split services when deploy risk, team boundaries, or scaling needs justify the operational cost. The code matters. The decisions behind the code matter more.

items.title: React Hooks
items.summary: Before hooks, you either wrote a simple function with no state or a class component with lifecycle methods and boilerplate. Hooks let you keep functions and still remember things. That changed how I structure components.

sections.content: React Hooks
Before hooks, functional components could not hold state. Class components could, but lifecycle methods and boilerplate piled up fast.
Hooks let functional components use state and side effects. useState remembers values. useEffect runs code after render. Custom hooks extract logic you reuse across files.
1. What Hooks Actually Are
Hooks are functions whose names start with use. They connect functional components to React features that used to require classes.
useState is a value plus a setter. useEffect runs after paint. Each hook has a narrow job.
2. Why Hooks Changed Everything
Hooks removed the either-or choice: simple function with no state, or class with ceremony. Logic also moves into custom hooks instead of copy-paste between components.
Extract shared logic once. Import the hook wherever you need the same behavior.
3. useState: Your State Management Tool
useState is the hook you will reach for most. Change the value, React re-renders the component.
4. useEffect: When You Need to Do Things
useEffect handles work outside pure rendering: fetch data, subscribe to events, clean up on unmount.
5. Performance Hooks: When You Need Speed
When renders get expensive, useMemo caches calculations and useCallback stabilizes function references. Use them when profiling shows a problem, not by default.
6. Custom Hooks: Your Secret Weapon
Custom hooks wrap state and effects into reusable functions. useFetchData, useLocalStorage, useForm: name them after what they do.
7. Context with Hooks: Sharing Data Made Easy
When many components need the same data, Context avoids passing props through every intermediate layer.
8. What You Should Actually Do
Start with useState and useEffect. Add useMemo and useCallback when measurements justify them. Call hooks at the top level, never inside conditions or loops.

items: Start with useState and useEffect - they're the most important
Create custom hooks for logic you use in multiple components
Use useMemo and useCallback only when you have performance issues
Follow the Rules of Hooks (always call them at the top level)
Give your hooks meaningful names that start with 'use'
Don't overthink it - start simple and add complexity later

sections.content: Start Building
Try a counter, a todo list, a small data-fetch hook, and a controlled form. Break things on purpose while learning.

items: Build a simple counter with useState
Create a todo list with useState and useEffect
Make a custom hook for fetching data from an API
Try building a form with controlled inputs using useState
Experiment with useMemo on a component that does heavy calculations

sections.content: Hooks are organization, not magic. Once the rules feel natural, most new React code stays in functions with hooks.
Final Thoughts
Hooks organize state and effects inside functions. Learn useState and useEffect first, then add custom hooks when the same logic appears in multiple files.

items.title: Performance Optimization: When Your App Starts to Crawl
items.summary: The app felt fast on your laptop. Then real users arrived on older phones and slow networks, and the complaints started. Performance work begins with measurement, not guessing.

sections.content: Performance Optimization: When Your App Starts to Crawl
The app felt fast on your machine. Then real users arrived on older phones and slow networks. Complaints followed. Performance work starts with measurement.
Most slowdowns come from a few familiar places. Find the bottleneck before rewriting components.
1. Measure First, Optimize Later
You cannot fix what you cannot see. Profile first with DevTools, Lighthouse, or React Profiler. The slow part is often not where you assumed.
Use Chrome DevTools or React DevTools to see what actually costs time. Guessing wastes hours.
2. The Usual Suspects: Common Performance Killers
Repeated database queries, huge renders, unoptimized images, naive algorithms, and missing caches show up again and again.

items: Too many database queries (especially N+1 problems)
Rendering too much at once (especially in React)
Loading too many images or assets
Inefficient algorithms (like searching through unsorted data)
Not using caching when you should

sections.content: 3. Smart Algorithms: The Big Wins
Choosing the right algorithm matters. Searching a sorted list with binary search beats scanning every item when data grows.
Binary search on sorted data reduces steps dramatically compared to linear scan at scale.
4. Caching: Don't Do the Same Work Twice
If the same API response is requested repeatedly, store it in memory or Redis instead of hitting the database every time.
Cache data that changes infrequently. Users notice when the same fetch runs on every navigation.
5. Async Programming: Don't Wait Around
Blocking the main thread on I/O makes the UI feel frozen. async/await keeps the interface responsive while work continues in the background.
Database and network calls should be asynchronous. The UI should not wait silently for seconds.
6. Fewer Requests = Faster Apps
Combine assets where possible. Lazy-load images and routes the user has not opened yet.
Defer work until it is needed. Initial load improves when you stop shipping code for screens nobody visited.
7. React-Specific Optimizations
React re-renders propagate by default. memo, useMemo, and useCallback help when profiling shows unnecessary work.
React.memo: Skip Re-renders When You Can
React.memo skips re-render when props are unchanged.
useMemo and useCallback: Cache Expensive Work
useMemo and useCallback cache values and functions between renders. They have overhead; use them deliberately.
Do not sprinkle memo hooks everywhere. Measure first.
Code Splitting: Load Only What You Need
Split routes and heavy components with React.lazy and Suspense so the first bundle stays small.
Virtualization: Handle Large Lists Like a Pro
Render only visible rows in long lists. react-window and similar libraries keep DOM size manageable.
8. Database Performance: The Hidden Killer
Slow queries often hurt more than front-end tweaks. Index fields you filter on. Avoid N+1 fetches.

items: Add indexes to fields you search frequently
Avoid N+1 queries - fetch related data in one query
Use connection pooling to reuse database connections
Cache frequently accessed data
Use read replicas for heavy read workloads

sections.content: 9. Images and Assets: The Heavy Stuff
Images dominate page weight. Compress them, serve modern formats, lazy-load below the fold, use a CDN when traffic spreads geographically.

items: Use WebP or AVIF instead of JPEG/PNG when possible
Use srcset for responsive images
Compress images - tools like TinyPNG work great
Use a CDN for faster delivery
Lazy load images that aren't immediately visible

sections.content: 10. Keep an Eye on Things
Performance degrades quietly as features accumulate. Monitor Core Web Vitals and set alerts before users report slowness.

items: Use Chrome DevTools to profile your app
Set up performance monitoring in production
Get alerts when things get slow
Run Lighthouse audits regularly
Track Core Web Vitals for user experience

sections.content: What You Should Actually Do
Measure, fix the largest bottleneck, cache stable data, optimize images, add memoization only where needed, then monitor again.

items: Measure first - use DevTools to find the real bottlenecks
Fix the biggest problems first - usually database queries or too many renders
Add caching for data that doesn't change often
Use async/await for slow operations
Optimize images and reduce HTTP requests
Use React.memo and useMemo when you actually need them
Set up monitoring so you know when things break

sections.content: Start Here
Run a performance audit, fix the slowest operation, cache one hot query, compress your largest assets, and add basic monitoring.

items: Open Chrome DevTools and run a performance audit on your app
Look for the slowest operations and fix those first
Add some basic caching to your most frequent database queries
Optimize your biggest images
Set up basic performance monitoring

sections.content: Optimize one problem at a time. Ship the fix, read the graph, move to the next bottleneck.

items.title: The Virtual DOM: React's Secret to Speed
items.summary: Updating the real DOM directly forces the browser to recalculate layout more than you need. React keeps a lightweight copy in memory and only patches what changed.

sections.content: The Virtual DOM: React's Secret to Speed
Touching the real DOM directly triggers layout and paint work across more nodes than you often need. React keeps a lightweight tree in memory and patches only the diff.
1. What the Virtual DOM Actually Is
The virtual tree is a JavaScript representation of UI. React compares the new tree to the previous one and updates the real DOM in minimal steps.
2. Why You Should Care About This
Direct DOM updates rewrite more than necessary. React's diff limits work to changed nodes.
3. How React's Diffing Actually Works
React compares old and new virtual trees, computes a minimal change set, and applies it. That diff step is where much of the performance comes from.
4. The Real Benefits You'll Notice
You describe what the UI should look like. React figures out how to update the DOM. You stop manually tracking every DOM mutation.
5. Keys: The Secret to Efficient Lists
Lists need stable keys so React knows which item moved, changed, or was removed. Without keys, React may re-render more than required.
Use stable unique keys from your data. Avoid array index as key when items reorder or delete.
6. Performance Tips That Actually Matter
React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, and sensible keys reduce unnecessary work. Profile before optimizing.

items: React.memo - prevents components from re-rendering when props haven't changed
useMemo - caches expensive calculations
useCallback - keeps function references stable
Proper keys - helps React track list items efficiently
Avoid creating objects in render - prevents unnecessary re-renders

sections.content: 7. Virtual DOM vs Real DOM: The Real Difference
The virtual tree is plain JavaScript objects. The real DOM triggers layout and paint. React batches updates to reduce thrashing.

items: Virtual DOM is fast because it's just JavaScript objects
Real DOM is slow because it triggers browser reflows and repaints
Virtual DOM lets you think declaratively (what should it look like?)
Real DOM forces you to think imperatively (how do I change it?)
Virtual DOM batches updates for better performance

sections.content: 8. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
Common mistakes: index keys on dynamic lists, new objects created inside render, over-memoization before measuring.

items: Don't use array indices as keys unless the list never changes
Don't create objects or functions inside render methods
Don't over-optimize - React is already pretty fast
Do use React.memo for components that re-render frequently
Do use useMemo and useCallback when you actually need them

sections.content: 9. Debugging: When Things Go Wrong
React DevTools and the Profiler show which components re-render and how long they take.

items: Install React Developer Tools - it's a major shift
Add console.log to see when components render
Use React Profiler to find performance bottlenecks
Check for missing or duplicate keys in lists
Look for objects being created in render methods

sections.content: What's Next?
Build a small todo app and watch updates in DevTools. Toggle memo on a hot component and compare render counts.

items: Build a simple todo app and watch how React updates the DOM
Try adding console.log to see when components re-render
Experiment with React.memo on a component that renders frequently
Create a list with and without proper keys to see the difference
Use React Developer Tools to explore your component tree

sections.content: The virtual DOM is engineering, not magic. Understand the diff and keys, and debugging render issues gets straightforward.

items.title: React Components, State, and Props: The Building Blocks
items.summary: A React app is small pieces with one job each: a button handles clicks, a card shows a user, a list renders rows. Components, state, and props are how those pieces connect.

sections.content: React Components, State, and Props: The Building Blocks
A React screen is built from small functions that return UI. A button, a card, a list row. You compose them into pages instead of one giant HTML file.
Each component owns one concern. Buttons handle clicks. Cards display records. Lists map data to rows.
1. Components: Your UI Building Blocks
A component is a function that returns markup. Reuse it wherever the same UI appears.
Break the page into focused pieces instead of one file that does everything.
Functional Components: The Modern Way
Functional components are the default. Learn classes only when you maintain older codebases.
Class Components: The Old Way (Don't Worry About These)
Class components still exist in legacy projects. New work should stay in functions with hooks.
2. State: When Your Component Needs to Remember Things
State is what a component remembers. When it changes, React re-renders to reflect the new value.
A counter stores its number in state. Each click updates state and the display follows.
useState: The Hook That Changes Everything
useState returns a value and a setter. Call the setter; React schedules a re-render.
Props: How Components Talk to Each Other
Props pass data from parent to child. The child reads them; the parent owns changes.
3. Props: Passing Data Down
Props are inputs to a component, like function arguments. They flow down, not up.
Simple Props Example
Parent passes message down. Child renders it. One direction keeps data flow traceable.
4. State vs Props: The Key Difference
State is internal and mutable via setters. Props are external inputs the child does not modify.
5. Component Composition: Building Big Things from Small Parts
Combine small components into layouts: header, sidebar, content, footer. Composition scales better than mega-components.
6. Common Patterns You'll Use Every Day
These patterns appear in most apps: fetch on mount, pass results to children, conditional loading states.
7. What You Should Actually Do
Keep components small. Use state for changing data, props for inputs, names that explain intent.

items: Keep components small - one job per component
Use functional components with hooks
Use state for data that changes
Use props for data that doesn't change
Give your components and props meaningful names
Don't overthink it - start simple and add complexity later

sections.content: Start Building
Build a counter, a todo list, a profile card, and a simple form. Practice beats reading.

items: Build a simple counter app with useState
Create a todo list with components, state, and props
Make a user profile card that receives data through props
Try building a simple form with controlled inputs
Experiment with conditional rendering (show/hide elements)

sections.content: Components, state, and props are the foundation. Everything else in React builds on those three ideas.
Components, state, and props are the foundation. Build small examples until moving data between pieces feels natural.

items.title: A Deep Dive into React
items.summary: What started as a clean component sometimes becomes a five-hundred-line file that does everything. These are the React concepts I return to when I need to untangle that.

sections.content: A Deep Dive into React
A component that started at fifty lines can grow to five hundred when every feature lands in one file. Understanding React fundamentals helps you split it back apart.
These are the concepts I return to on real projects: components, the virtual DOM, hooks, performance, and state sharing.
1. Components: Your Building Blocks
Components are functions that return UI. Combine a button, a card, and a list into a screen. Data flow and updates happen through props and state.
useState tells React this component remembers a value that can change. Click the button, count updates, only this subtree re-renders.
2. The Virtual DOM: React's Secret Weapon
React does not write to the real DOM on every state change. It diffs a virtual tree and patches the minimum.
Adding one list item updates that row, not the entire list, when keys and structure are correct.
3. Hooks
Hooks brought state and effects to functional components without class lifecycle noise.
useEffect with an empty dependency array runs once on mount. Fetch user data there, store in state, render when ready.
4. Performance: Don't Re-render Everything
Parent re-renders can cascade to children even when their props are identical. memo and useMemo address that when profiling confirms waste.
React.memo prevents re-render when props are shallow-equal.
5. State Management: When Props Aren't Enough
When props drilling gets deep, Context shares data across subtrees. Redux helps when updates are complex and global.
Redux adds structure: actions describe events, reducers compute new state. Reach for Context first; add Redux when complexity demands it.
6. Advanced Patterns: The Pro Moves
Advanced patterns solve specific problems. Adopt them when you hit the problem, not before.
Context suits theme, auth, and locale: data many components read, few components write.
Custom Hooks: Your Secret Weapon
Custom hooks move repeated useEffect and useState logic into one reusable function.
Error Boundaries: Graceful Failure
Error boundaries catch render errors in a subtree and show fallback UI instead of a white screen.
Testing: Don't Skip This
Tests on critical interactions save debugging time later. Start with user-visible behavior, not implementation details.
React Router
React Router maps URLs to components for multi-view single-page apps.
Performance Tips That Actually Matter
Most performance issues are too many renders or too much data at once. Fix those before micro-optimizing.
What You Should Actually Build Next
Build a todo app, a weather fetcher, or a filtered product list. One real project teaches more than reading alone.

items: A simple todo app with add, edit, delete, and mark complete functionality
A weather app that fetches data from an API and displays it nicely
A small e-commerce product list with filtering and search
A blog with posts, comments, and user authentication
A real-time chat application using WebSockets

sections.content: Final Thoughts
React rewards understanding over memorization. Write working code first, refactor when friction appears.
The community is large. Ask questions when stuck. Every senior engineer started with broken first commits.
Pick one small project and finish it. Completion teaches more than collecting patterns.

items.title: Why I Chose React Over Angular or Vue
items.summary: I built the same kinds of projects in React, Angular, and Vue. All three work. React matched how I think about UI: small components, one-way data, and freedom to pick tools as the app grows.

sections.content: Why I Chose React Over Angular or Vue
I tried React, Angular, and Vue on similar projects. All three ship production software. React matched how I think about UI composition and incremental complexity.
React balanced power and flexibility for the teams I was on. Angular and Vue are solid; this is what fit my workflow.
1. Components as Building Blocks
React components are reusable UI functions. Write a product card once, use it on every listing page.
Angular and Vue have components too. React's function-first model felt natural for the way I split screens.
On an e-commerce site, one ProductCard component replaces copied markup across pages.
2. One-Way Data Flow: No Surprises
React favors one-way data flow: props down, events up. When something breaks, you trace data in one direction.
Two-way binding can be convenient but harder to reason about in large trees. Explicit flow helped me debug faster.
A chat app keeps messages in parent state and passes them to list and input children.
3. Virtual DOM: Smart Updates
React diffs a virtual DOM and patches minimal changes. That matters when lists update frequently.
Vue uses a virtual DOM as well. Angular relies on change detection. I preferred React's predictable update model in the apps I maintained.
A news feed appending posts benefits from targeted updates instead of repainting the whole list.
4. Freedom to Build Your Way
React does not prescribe routing, state, or styling. You add tools as requirements appear.
Angular bundles more opinions upfront, which helps some teams and overwhelms others on day one.
Third-party libraries integrate as components without fighting framework conventions.
5. Great Tools and Community
React DevTools expose component trees, props, and state. That visibility shortened debug sessions.
A large community means most errors have prior art on Stack Overflow or GitHub.
Mix local useState with Redux in the same component when different slices need different scope.
6. Easy to Get Started
You can ship a Hello component on day one and add hooks as features require them.
Angular often expects TypeScript, modules, and DI from the start. React lets you grow into structure.
7. Jobs and Community
React has a large community and strong job market. Meta maintains the core library. When you get stuck, someone has usually hit the same error before.

items: Huge community - someone has solved your problem
Lots of job opportunities
Regular updates from Meta
Tons of tutorials and resources
Great libraries for everything
Active community on Stack Overflow

sections.content: 8. Performance: React Keeps It Fast
React's bundle size and runtime performance are competitive for large apps. React.memo and route-level code splitting keep re-renders and initial load in check.
Memoized list items skip re-render when their props stay the same. That pattern matters on feeds and tables that update often.
Quick Comparison
A quick read on each framework:

items: React: Flexible, great for teams, huge ecosystem, easy to start
Angular: Full-featured, TypeScript-first, lots of built-in stuff, steeper learning curve
Vue: Easy to learn, good for small projects, smaller ecosystem

sections.content: When to Pick Each One
All three are valid choices. Match the framework to team experience, project size, and how much opinionated structure you want upfront.

items: Pick React for: Flexibility, large teams, complex UIs, mobile apps (React Native)
Pick Angular for: Enterprise apps, TypeScript teams, lots of built-in features
Pick Vue for: Small projects, quick prototypes, easy learning curve

sections.content: Final Thoughts
React fit my projects because components stayed small and data flow stayed explicit. If you are still deciding, build the same feature in each framework and notice which one gets out of your way.

metadata.title: Again Tomorrow
metadata.author: Ansumana Darboe
metadata.subtitle: From red earth to React, and everything in between

sections.content:
I have lived in two countries, spoken six languages, played football professionally, taught children in a crowded rural classroom where they shared desks and textbooks, and debugged code at two in the morning with cold coffee sitting next to my keyboard. I am still not sure which of those things surprised me most.

This is the story of how they connect. I wrote it for my child. For my family. And for you, if you have ever looked at someone else's life and wondered how it all came together.

I will keep it honest. Some of it is funny, in the way things are only funny after they are over. Some of it was hard, in the way things are hard when you are the only person who knows how hard they are. But most of it is just life; the small, specific, unremarkable moments that turn out, looking back, to be the whole thing.
When I started writing this, my mother was already gone. I am not going to tell you how yet.
The Compound

sections.alt: Young Ansumana in The Gambia village
sections.caption: The compound, The Gambia

sections.content:
I was born in Dumbuto, a small village in The Gambia. If you have never been to a West African village, the first thing you notice is the earth. It is genuinely red, the color of rust when the rains come. The second thing is the sound: roosters before the sun is up, goats in the compound, the low percussion of someone pounding grain in the early morning, my mother calling me before I was ready to be called.

My father worked for the Deutsche Gesellschaft fur Technische Zusammenarbeit, the GTZ. He managed three nature reserves in the Gambia Forest Park, which meant he left the house with red earth on his boots and came back with more of it. He carried a walkie-talkie for the reserves. In the house, on his desk, there was a desktop computer. He was a quiet man. Not distant. Quiet. There is a difference. He could sit through an entire dinner without saying anything and still be the most present person at the table. When he spoke, you stopped whatever you were doing.

"Ansumana," he said once, in the compound, in the late afternoon when the light goes orange. "A man's worth is not measured by what he has, but by what he gives to others." He said it once. He never repeated it. He did not need to.

My mother was something else entirely. She farmed and raised children at the same time, which sounds manageable until you actually watch someone do it. She taught without lecturing, a rare quality I did not appreciate until I was much older and realized how uncommon it is. She would take me to the fields and show me how to plant a seed. Not too deep, not too shallow. She explained that this was how you did everything in life. Then she kept working. No pause for effect. No waiting to see if the lesson had landed. Just the next task.

I do not remember ever sitting at a meal with just the people who lived in our house. There was always someone else; a cousin passing through, a neighbour whose cooking fire had not been lit that evening, someone's auntie whose name I was supposed to know and usually did. The bowl went in the middle. Everyone ate from it. No one announced this as generosity. It was simply how meals worked.

Every adult in the village could also correct any child, and they did. You did not talk back. This was not harshness; it was consistency. The expectation was the same from every direction: carry yourself properly. I understood this long before I could explain it.

I was about five the first time I understood what community actually meant. I was playing near the village well with some friends when I knocked a bucket of water onto the ground. Water is not cheap in a village without running taps. I froze. Just stood there watching it soak into the dry earth, knowing whatever was coming was coming.
Mba Fatou, she lived three compounds down from us and was always in the same blue wrapper, saw what happened. She called my name. I walked over slowly.

She took my hands in hers. "Come," she said. That was all. She walked me to the well, pulled up a full bucket herself, and handed it to me to carry back. We made the whole walk in silence. When we reached the compound she let go and went back to whatever she had been doing before I spilled the water. She did not shout. She did not tell my mother. She just made me replace what I had wasted and left me to think about the rest myself.

If you are reading this and your first reaction to the words 'grew up in The Gambia' is sympathy, spare it. Growing up there was one of the better things that happened to me. The Gambia is called the Smiling Coast, and this is not just a tourism slogan. If you arrive as a stranger at mealtime, someone will invite you to eat. They mean it. A bowl in the middle of the compound, everyone sitting around it, nobody eating alone. That is not poverty. That is a different set of priorities.

My family is Mandinka. I grew up playing with Wolof friends, Fula friends, Jola friends, Serer friends. I speak four local languages from that upbringing, along with English and German. Most of us spoke at least two local languages before we learned any English. When you grow up like that, moving easily between languages and customs, you stop thinking of difference as a problem to solve.

Some use spoons today; what matters is that no one eats alone. That is a principle, not a tradition. It travels with you.

I did not know, then, that I was being shaped. That is the thing about those early years. Nobody announces it. You are just there, living, playing, getting corrected by Mba Fatou, watching your father come home with dirt on his boots. And then one day you are somewhere else entirely, and you realize all of it came with you.
The Real School

Some mornings the animals were more work than others.

The dry season was manageable. But when the rains came and the ground turned soft, moving the goats before school became a proper negotiation. They did not want to go where I wanted them to go. I did not want to be late. Neither of us won completely.

I was maybe eight or nine. I cannot remember exactly. What I do remember is the weight of the milk container on the walk back, trying not to spill it, and the way the herdsman always looked at me like he was deciding whether I was ready to be trusted with this without him. I was never quite sure I was.

When chores were done and school was over, the afternoons were ours. We ran barefoot on sandy paths; our feet the color of the earth by evening, which meant our mothers could always tell how far we had wandered. We played suwe, hopscotch drawn in the dirt with a stick. We played hide and seek between the trees. And we played football.

Football was different from the others. Football had rules.

The girls played Piribong, a rope jumping game that needed at least three people; two holding the ends while others jumped in. Rhythm, timing, coordination. Harder than it looked. They also played Zuu, which involved throwing and running from a slipper. You had to be fast and smart. Zuu was not for the slow.

I do not know exactly when the football rules were established. There was no meeting. Nobody wrote them down. You simply arrived on the pitch one afternoon and they were already there, as natural as the ground under your feet. Older boys had brought them. Boys before them had carried them from somewhere. That is how it worked.

If you were new and you broke one, you learned immediately. The whole game stopped. Twenty pairs of eyes. No words needed.

items: The owner of the ball is the king. If he gets tired, the game ends.
The chubby kid is always the goalkeeper.
No matter the score, the team that scores the last goal wins the game.
If an elderly person is passing, the game stops until they pass.
A ball stuck under a car is the worst thing ever.
If the ball owner gets angry, the game is over.
The best player is always on the same team as the ball owner.
The two best players can't play on the same team, so everyone chooses their players. Being chosen last is a humiliation.
If the ball owner has to do chores, other players help finish quickly.
To start a game, we always said "Epp the game begins" and kicked the ball in the air.
The player who scores the most amazing goal feels better than Ronaldo.
One kid always plays in expensive boots and everyone hates him.
The goalkeeper wears slippers as gloves.
It's all massive attack, massive defence.
