The rule that caused the most problems was always the first one.

We had a boy on our street who owned a proper ball; real leather, properly pumped. In our world that made him something close to royalty. He was not the best player. He was not even close to the best player. But his ball was real and ours was rags, so we called him by his nickname and we told him he had played well even when he had not, and we kept our complaints to ourselves.

One evening he got annoyed about something. A bad foul, maybe. Or nobody passing to him enough. I honestly do not remember. What I remember is him bending down, picking up his ball, tucking it under his arm, and walking home without a word.

Fifteen of us just standing there. The game was over. You could do nothing except watch him go and hope tomorrow he was in a better mood.

Saturday evenings were for the campfire. Both boys and girls, which was unusual; we spent most of the week in our separate worlds. But the campfire was different. Someone would start a song and everyone else found their way in, whether they could sing or not. I could not sing. I have never been able to sing. But at a campfire in the dark with everyone else going, it did not really matter.

I had a song dedicated to me. Two, if I am being accurate. I am not going to say what they were. Some things are better kept.

Friday evenings were the grandparents. The whole family gathered and they talked; not gossip, but stories. The kind that explained why certain things were the way they were. Why a particular road curved the way it did. What a relative had done generations ago that people still brought up. I would sit completely still during these sessions, which anyone who knew me as a child would tell you was unusual. Something about the way the grandparents spoke made you feel that moving would break something.

The elders saw everything. Every adult in the community could call you by name, correct you in the street, send you home without explanation. There was a retired teacher on our street who seemed to exist purely to notice when boys were doing things they should not be doing. His timing was impossible. You would think of something mischievous and he would appear. We were completely convinced he had a system.

When Tobaski came, you went back to the village. Not because anyone demanded it. Because you wanted to. The line between nuclear and extended family barely existed; grandparents, aunties, uncles, cousins; everyone close, or showing up as if they were. Childcare shared. Food shared. If you needed something and someone had it, you had it.

I was always being taught. I just did not know it at the time. The mornings with the animals, the afternoons on the pitch, the Friday evenings with the grandparents; all of it was building something. You could not see what it was building. You were too busy being inside it.
The Youngest in the Room

The first day of school I discovered I was the youngest in my class.

Not by a small amount. By what felt, at that age, like a significant amount. The others were already taller, already settled, already talking to each other like they had known each other for years, which some of them had. I sat down at my desk and kept my bag on my lap for a long time, as if I might still need it to leave quickly.

Nobody mentioned that I was the youngest. They did not need to. You could just see it.

The school building was low and rectangular, with a corrugated iron roof that turned rain into percussion. On quiet mornings you could hear a lesson happening in the room next to yours. On rainy days you could hear nothing at all except the roof. The blackboard was cracked in two places and the teacher worked around it without comment, writing on the parts that still held chalk and leaving the rest alone. The desks were wooden, worn smooth by years of elbows and arms and people waiting for time to pass.

We had a teacher who kept a long wooden cane on his desk. Not for measuring anything. It sat there the way objects sit on desks when they are meant to be noticed.

I was never sure if he believed in it as a system or simply found it useful. Either way, the classroom was quiet. The classroom paid attention. Whether that came from genuine interest or from keeping one eye on the desk, I cannot honestly say. Probably both, depending on the day and depending on the student.

Being the youngest meant working harder to keep up. After school, when chores were done, I would sit under the neem tree at the edge of the compound and go through the day's work again. Not because someone told me to. Because being the youngest meant there were gaps, and gaps have a way of growing if you leave them alone.

My friends played nearby. I could hear them clearly; I was not that far away. Some evenings I would look up and watch for a moment, then look back down. The tree gave good shade. The light lasted longer than you expected. Those were the two things working in my favour.

At home I took things apart. Broken radios, old bicycles, whatever I could find that moved or lit up or made noise. My mother was not always pleased about this. I put most of it back together. (Not always successfully.)

After primary school and Kwinella Junior Secondary School, I moved to Kombo to live with my uncle and attend Muslim High School in Banjul.

The bus there took longer than I expected. I sat in the back and watched the landscape change; the red earth of home giving way to paved roads and buildings pressed against each other and cars moving with a kind of urgency I was not used to. I pressed my face to the window for most of the journey. I was trying to remember what I was looking at, knowing I would want to describe it to someone later.

My uncle's house had rules. Punctuality. Meals at a certain time. How you presented yourself before leaving the house in the morning. He did not state these rules the way a list would be stated. He lived by them himself and then noticed, quietly, when you did not.

I learned to be on time. I learned to tuck in my shirt. I learned that some people express care through standards rather than softness, and that both are genuine.

Muslim High School had a reputation, and the reputation was accurate. The first week I mostly sat and watched; how the others wrote, how they asked questions, how they handled being called on when they did not know the answer.

I fell in love with mathematics that year. Not straight away. It took about three weeks. But something clicked in those early classes; the way numbers had rules that never changed, the way you could trust a process to arrive somewhere reliable. Everything else in my life had variables. Mathematics was the one place where following the steps correctly guaranteed the result.

There were students with more than me. Better materials. Books at home. Some had been tutored privately; you could tell by how quickly they answered, without any visible working-out. (This irritated me at the time. I understand it better now.)

What I had was the habit of sitting with something until it made sense. From all those evenings under the neem tree. That turned out to matter more than I expected it to.

Every new school, every new teacher, every new city asked something different from me. Moving to Kombo meant adapting faster than felt comfortable. The school year was already moving and you either caught the current or you fell behind.

I caught it. Not elegantly. But I caught it.
Again Tomorrow

My boots were always dusty. Even on the days we played on grass, which were not many, the dust found its way back by the end of the game.

I was maybe twelve or thirteen when football stopped feeling like play and started feeling like the thing I was supposed to do. I could not have explained that at the time. I just knew that when the game ended, I was already thinking about the next one. I could not imagine a week without it.

Moving to Kombo changed things. I joined a local team and started training properly; the smell of the grass when we were lucky enough to be on grass, the feel of a real ball under my boots, my teammates calling out plays in the heat. We trained in the rain sometimes. I came home muddy in a way that meant the session had gone well.

I did not become good quickly. I became good by showing up more than anyone else wanted to. Mornings before school. Evenings on the pitch until the light went.

Our coach was not a man of speeches. He had one phrase he used after any session he considered poor. "Again tomorrow." That was it. He said it without looking at us, picked up his bag, and walked off the pitch. At fifteen I found this deeply unsatisfying. It took me years, in different countries, learning entirely different things, to understand that "again tomorrow" was the only honest thing a coach could say.

There is one match I still see clearly. A local cup semi-final, mid-afternoon, the pitch already hard from days without rain. The crowd was mostly people who knew someone on the pitch; aunties under umbrellas, boys selling water in plastic bags, heat on the back of your neck and dust in your throat.

We were down 1-0 at halftime. Our striker had missed a sitter I had set up. I was angry at him and at myself for being angry, which is a familiar football feeling.

Second half. Whistle. I took the ball on the left, beat one defender, then another. The second one grabbed my shirt and I still have the scar on my elbow from where I hit the ground when he let go. I got up. Pass inside. Shot. Goal.

The sound that followed was not polite applause. It was the compound version of a roar. People standing. Someone blowing a whistle they were not supposed to have.

We lost on penalties. I missed the fourth one. The ball went over the bar and the silence was worse than the noise had been. I walked to the bench and sat down. My coach said nothing for a long time. Then: "Again tomorrow."

That match did not make me a professional. It made me remember why I kept coming back.

Eventually I played professionally for just over four years. We won two major trophies and finished runner-up in a third competition. I also served as player-coach for our youth team, which meant I had to learn a completely different skill: staying quiet while someone made a mistake I could see coming from twenty yards away, and waiting until after to explain why.

The injury happened during an intense match. A collision; nothing unusual, the kind that happens fifty times a season. But this one was different. I heard it before I felt it. Then I was on the ground and my teammates were crowding around and the sky above them was very bright and very still, and someone was asking me something I could not quite hear.

Torn ligament. Months of rehabilitation. No playing. The doctor was kind about it, which made it worse somehow.

I was angry for a while. Not at anyone in particular. Just angry the way you are when something that defined you is suddenly past tense. The empty afternoons were the hard part. Then, after a few weeks, I started doing other things with the time I had. The knee healed. Not back to what it was. But enough. I stopped playing competitively. I started watching the game differently, studying it rather than being inside it. What I had built on that pitch did not disappear. It went somewhere else.
Forty Children

Forty children looked up when I walked in on that first morning.

I remember noticing how quiet forty children could be when they were genuinely uncertain about someone. The room was small. It smelled of chalk and sweat and heat that had nowhere to go. No fan. Just old wooden desks, worn smooth by years of elbows, and not enough of them. Some children shared a desk. Textbooks went between hands; one copy for three or four children on a good day.

I managed Neil Williams Nursery School and later taught at a primary school in rural Gambia. Cracked blackboards. Materials that ran out by October. But the children were there. All of them. All at once. Looking at me the same way I had once looked at a teacher standing in the front of a room just like this one.

I was twenty-something and used to being the person who performed. In that room I was just the adult who had to figure it out. That took a few weeks to get used to.

Teaching in rural Gambia meant working with what was there, which was not much. Small classrooms. Old desks. Children sharing seats. Textbooks shared until the covers came loose. Basic supplies unreliable. You became creative out of necessity, not virtue. I used local materials. I used my hands. I drew on the board more than any teacher probably should.

What frustrated me was not the children. It was the gap between what they needed and what the room had. No printer. No photocopier. The same lesson on the board three days running because there was nothing to hand out. A parent who could not afford notebooks asking if their child could share. You swallowed that and kept going. What surprised me was how fast things changed when a child finally had your full attention. Not weeks. Sometimes days.

"Good morning, class," I said, standing at the front of the room. "Good morning, Mr. Darboe," they chorused back, their voices doing the thing children's voices do when they say something all at once.

There was one boy who sat at the back of the room during those first weeks. Not because he was asked to. The back was where you sat when you were afraid of being called on. By the third week I understood why. He could not read. Not a word. Nobody had said anything, which is not always the same thing as nobody having noticed. I moved his desk to the front. By the end of the term he could read a full paragraph; slowly, sounding out each word, but reading. The day it happened he looked up when he reached the end, not at me, just at the space in front of him, like he was not entirely sure the words had come from him. I gave him the next page without making anything of it.

Teaching gave me a patience I did not know I needed. Every day brought students who were struggling with something I had once struggled with, parents who could not afford what their children needed, the constant arithmetic of doing more with less. But every day also had the moment when a child reads a full sentence for the first time; out loud, slowly, their face changing as they realize they have done it. (That expression. There is nothing else quite like it.)

There were afternoons when I was not patient enough. When the room was too hot and the materials were not there and I answered a child too sharply.

I still think about some of those students. Wonder what they are doing now. I loved teaching. But I knew, eventually, that I wanted to do something else. Not instead of giving back. Alongside it. I just had not found it yet.
Hello World

Mr. Nyabally did not look like someone who was about to change the direction of my life. But then, they rarely do.

The year was 2008. I had enrolled at the Gambia Technical Training Institute; GTTI; to study software applications. This was not a casual decision. The truth is, I had been thinking about computers since I was a child sitting in front of my father's desktop while he was at work. We were not allowed to touch it. I touched it. I found the games. I played them until I heard the gate, and then I left the chair exactly as I had found it and went back outside. My father never said anything. Either he did not notice, or he decided not to. I have always suspected the second one. Either way, that machine was the first computer I understood, even if only as a thing that ran games and had to be treated with a particular kind of respect.

The computer lab at GTTI had machines that were slow and old, keyboards that clicked loudly in the quiet. You could hear every keystroke. The first day I sat down in front of one and felt something I can only describe as alertness; the kind where your whole body is paying attention without being told to.

"Today," Mr. Nyabally said, standing at the front of the lab, "we are going to write our first program. It is called Hello World, and it is the traditional first program that every programmer writes."

He typed slowly, deliberately. He ran the program. Two words appeared on the screen.

Hello World.

I leaned forward. He had typed something and something had appeared. The machine had done exactly what it was told. I felt my heart move in a way I was not expecting. I wanted to do that. I needed to do that.

From that day I spent every spare minute in the lab. Trying commands. Breaking things. Fixing what I could and asking about what I could not. I once deleted a file I could not restore and sat in the lab until they closed it. I stayed after class until they closed the lab. (Sometimes slightly after.)

Between June 2008 and November 2010, I built a foundation in JavaScript, C, C++, HTML, and CSS; and in the principles behind how computers think. I also served as Class Representative, which meant learning how to sit between two sides, students and administration, and help them understand each other. That turned out to be useful later, in ways I did not expect.
I still type a little too hard on keyboards. Mr. Nyabally would probably notice.
Quarter Past Nine

My first real job in tech was at AccounTax Solutions LLC in Gambia, starting July 2011. I was responsible for the IT setup for a 50-person team; networks, file servers, workstations, internet access. I had never done this at this scale before. (I did not mention this.)

Part of my job was training the team on software and workflows. I remember someone coming to me and saying, Ansumana, I do not know how to do this. We would sit together and I would show them step by step. Then they would come back later, excited, because they had figured something out on their own. That was always the better moment; not the showing, but the coming back.

When a network went down in an accounting firm, work stopped. Everything stopped. Accounting firms are quiet places until the internet stops. Then suddenly everyone has an opinion about DHCP.

Early on I misconfigured a server and took the file share offline for most of a morning. I fixed it. Nobody fired me. I did not forgive myself quickly.

After that I learned to diagnose problems quickly, to stay calm when people were standing behind me waiting, to think through things step by step while someone asked the same question three times. We maintained 99 percent system uptime. If your systems serve people doing real work, every minute of downtime is someone's problem, not just a number.

One project stays with me. The office was processing insurance claims by hand; slow, error-prone, people doing the same repetitive task all day. I suggested a simple database system that could automate most of it, built it in Linux with Excel and whatever programming I had from GTTI, and it took weeks. When it was finished, claims that had taken hours took minutes.

"Ansu." She turned her monitor toward me when the system was ready. She pulled up a claim, ran it through, and looked at the clock. "This used to take me until lunch." It was quarter past nine in the morning. She did not say anything else. She closed the window, opened another claim, and I understood the conversation was over. I stood there a moment, then went back to my desk.

I stayed at AccounTax until April 2013. Two years of networks, troubleshooting, and sitting with people who were scared of computers until they were not. I am still proud of those two years. They built habits that carried into everything that came next.

Then there was a year I spent in The Gambia working out what came next. Not a dramatic year. I took small IT jobs where I could find them. In the evenings I was on Codecademy, freeCodeCamp, w3schools, Stack Overflow, a mobile app called Sololearn. I read articles. I watched conference talks on YouTube from developers who seemed to live in a different world entirely. I thought about Berlin because someone I had met mentioned it, then kept thinking about it because I could not stop. The decision did not arrive all at once. It came in pieces, slowly, over months of sitting with it. I was not sure leaving was wise. I was sure I would regret it if I did not try. By the time I bought the ticket I had been thinking about it for the better part of a year.
April 2014

My breath was visible before I had even stepped all the way off the train.

I stopped in the middle of the platform, people moving around me in every direction, and just watched it happen. April 2014. Berlin Hauptbahnhof. I had known the cold was coming; Germany is not a secret; but knowing and experiencing are two separate things, and I learned this within thirty seconds of arrival. The ceiling of the station was far above me. The signs were in a language I could not read. I picked up my bag and kept moving, because that was the only thing left to do.

The first months were not a montage. They were long. I knew almost no one. My German was nowhere near useful yet. I would call home and then sit in the flat afterward without turning the lights on for a while, trying to decide whether loneliness was something you admitted out loud or just got on with.

What kept me here was not confidence. It was stubbornness that sometimes passed for patience.

I applied for things I was not ready for and was told no, politely, which is sometimes worse than being told no impolitely. One interview I remember clearly: I understood the technical question. I answered it in English. The interviewer switched to German. I understood the words individually. I could not make them into a sentence fast enough. I left and rode the U-Bahn for three extra stops because I did not want to get off yet.

Winter was not poetic. It was functional and cold and dark by four o'clock. I learned to layer clothes the way people in Berlin told me to, and I still misjudged it for the first two winters.

The first German joke I understood without translating it in my head arrived a year and a half in. My classmate said something about the BVG being on time, and the whole table laughed, and I laughed a second late, and then I understood why. That small delayed laugh felt like crossing a border.

The first thing I knew I had to do was learn German. You cannot build a life somewhere if you cannot speak. In February 2016 I enrolled at BSI Berlin Sprachenschule. I spent two years there.

Learning a language as an adult is humbling in a particular way. You feel intelligent in your own language. You feel like a child in someone else's. I sat in class listening to words that meant nothing, writing sentences that felt wrong the moment I put them down, asking people to repeat themselves more times than I wanted to count.

By January 2018 I had reached C1 level; speaking, writing, comprehension. I could have real conversations. I could understand jokes, which is the actual test of a language. I also took the Leben in Deutschland test and scored 33 out of 33. (I prepared seriously. I am not going to pretend I did not prepare seriously.) The small victory I actually remember: ordering food in a restaurant without pointing at the menu. The waiter did not switch to English out of pity. That felt like progress.

Once I felt confident in the language, I enrolled at the Digital Career Institute in March 2018. A full-stack development program covering the MERN stack; MongoDB, Express, React, and Node.js; alongside Agile methodologies and real web development practice. I could follow everything now. Ask questions without feeling lost. The two years at BSI had made the year at DCI possible.

At DCI I built the Buildy mobile app in React Native with two classmates, Sergio and Gaia; a tool that connected people with home renovation and design companies. When it launched, it reached over a thousand downloads and earned a 4.2-star rating. Real people were using something I had built. The first week was not clean. I had tested on my phone and assumed that was enough. That feeling does not get old.

Berlin had a tech community I did not expect; meetups, small events, people from everywhere building things together.

My first one was in a bar near Mitte that I found from a link someone had shared at DCI. I arrived early because I thought arriving early would help. It did not. Everyone seemed to already know everyone. I got a drink and stood near the wall for about twenty minutes. Then someone came over and asked what I was building. I told him about the Buildy app. He told me what he was working on. We stood there for another hour. By the time I left I had two new contacts and a slightly clearer sense that this city was not closed to me.

That is all belonging ever takes: one person who asks a real question and stays for the answer.
I think about Hauptbahnhof sometimes. The cold, the breath, the signs I could not read. It was not that long ago. It feels like a different person. But it was not.
In Berlin, the rooms got bigger. The person on the other end of the screen did not.
Signatures at Midnight

I joined Propstack GmbH in April 2019 for a short internship. My first startup. Real estate software; a React Native app for agents running open houses and listings across Germany.

Startups have a particular pace that either excites you or exhausts you. It excited me. You build quickly. You ship. You find out what works by releasing it to people who tell you, with their behavior, exactly what they think.

One agent, Klaus or something, used the old app during an open house. Mid-conversation with a couple who were ready to sign, the app crashed. Not a graceful crash. A white screen, spinning wheel, the particular silence of two people deciding whether to keep waiting. He called support while the clients looked at their phones.

I had shipped that sync logic. I was proud of it until that afternoon. We fixed it that night. A sync bug that only surfaced when you had weak signal and tried to upload photos in a specific order. I stayed until two in the morning reproducing it on a phone taped to the desk with bad WiFi. We shipped the patch before his next viewing on Saturday.

He sent a one-line email on Monday: "Worked." That was the whole review. Klaus never wrote about the app again. In customer relations, silence after "Worked" is practically a five-star review.

After Propstack I spent about sixteen months freelancing; smaller client projects, staying current, working out where I wanted to go next. Then March 2020 arrived and changed the shape of everything for a while. The pandemic made the job market contract and then, slowly, settle into something new. I kept learning. By September 2020 I had a clear next step.

change.org e.V. in Berlin. The office was small; the kind of place where you could hear every conversation and the coffee machine was always running. The coffee was not good. The petitions were. The platform itself was anything but small. About 500M people across the world used it to organize campaigns, collect signatures, and push for things they actually cared about. Every feature I built was connected to a real decision someone was trying to make. Someone starting a petition. Someone signing one at midnight because they could not sleep.

I was there from September 2020 to July 2022. Those were not easy years in ways that had nothing to do with code. But the work gave the days a shape, and that mattered.

In July 2022, the Germany team rebranded to innn.it and I stayed through the transition. We cut page load times from 8 seconds to 1.5 seconds. Written down, that is a technical achievement. What it actually was: someone on a slow mobile connection in a rural area could now open a campaign page without giving up halfway. When traffic spiked during a campaign, the system either held or it did not. I was wrong about readiness more than once before I got it right.

I stayed through July 2023. Nearly three years across both organisations. The team was good; the kind where you become a better developer simply from being around people who care. I wrote more carefully there than anywhere before it, because the culture made clarity feel worth the effort.
Friday Evenings

On Friday evenings in the village, my grandfather arranged us around him in the compound before he started speaking. There was a particular way he cleared his throat first. Even at seven or eight, sitting cross-legged on the ground while the sky moved from orange to dark above us, I understood this as a signal; the words coming were from somewhere important.

The stories were not entertainment. They carried things inside them: where we came from, what particular families had done and why, what we owed to each other. I could not have articulated any of this at that age. I just knew that I did not move until he was finished.

Roughly three decades later, I was sitting in a flat in Berlin, late in the evening in 2023, scrolling through children's apps on my laptop. The city outside was quiet. I kept scrolling and kept noticing the same gap.

Most of these platforms did not have stories for children who looked like the ones I grew up around. None of them carried what those Friday evenings had carried. I noticed this the way you notice an absence; not all at once, but slowly, and then more clearly each time. When a child only ever sees themselves in the stories they read, the people around them probably do not think about it. When they do not, the absence is something you feel rather than describe.

That July, my co-founder and I started building ZULA. A platform for diverse and inclusive children's stories. The idea did not come from a pitch deck. It came from something I kept seeing that was not there; and from a compound in the village, and an old man who cleared his throat before he spoke, and stories that had already traveled further than anyone sitting in that circle could have imagined.

We made wrong assumptions early. I thought if the stories were good enough, the rest would follow.

I built it mobile-first in React, React Native, Node.js, AWS, and MongoDB. We made it work offline and on low bandwidth connections, because the children who needed these stories most were often in places where connectivity was unreliable. We reached over 5,000 children across 15 countries.

We raised over 20,000 euros in funding. We partnered with Audible and other publishers to distribute over 300 printed books. And in September 2024 we pitched ZULA at the Afro German Startup Pitch in Hamburg, finishing third among more than a hundred applicants.

Third is not first. But third, when you started from nothing, is not bad. One judge asked how we would scale. I had a slide for that. I also had a spreadsheet that disagreed with the slide, politely.

ZULA ran from July 2023 to September 2024. Funding is a constraint that does not care about the quality of what you have built. We had stretched the budget as far as it would go; reduced costs, maintained uptime, kept growing. But the numbers eventually stopped working in our favour. September came and the decision was made. That is the honest version.

I think about those Friday evenings sometimes, and I wonder whether my grandfather had any sense that the stories he told in that compound would follow someone five thousand kilometres across a continent, decades later, and become the reason a product existed.

I suspect he did. That is the thing about people who tell stories with intention. They know the words travel further than the room.
She Put the Laptop Down

I have been at Frey ADV since October 2024 as a Senior Software Engineer. The project is called Quincy Mobile.

The task: take a desktop system that is 30 years old and turn it into something that works on a phone, a tablet, and a desktop browser. The people using it are doctors and medical staff; over a thousand of them, depending on it every day.

A 30-year-old system carries 30 years of decisions inside it. Some of them were sensible for their time. Some were less sensible even then. Some parts of the code looked old enough to have voted. Every legacy system has one function nobody wants to touch. We had several. You do not throw any of it away carelessly, because people's workflows; real people, trying to see patients and fill prescriptions and read results; are built around it.

Early on I sat with one of the doctors to understand how she moved through her day. I had prepared questions on my laptop. I did not get through many of them. She started talking and I put the laptop down and just listened. The system had been designed around a process that made sense to whoever built it in the 1980s, not to someone trying to see twelve patients before lunch. That conversation took about forty minutes. I came back to the team with more useful information than two weeks of reading the codebase had given me.

We moved the legacy app to React and TypeScript. Load times dropped noticeably in testing. Screens that had taken seconds to open started responding while you were still reaching for the mouse. One doctor told me she stopped keeping a paper backup list because the mobile view finally felt faster than writing things down by hand.

When you are building tools for people who handle someone else's health information, shortcuts are not a choice that belongs to you. The thing I noticed first was quieter: fewer support calls about tasks that should have been obvious, and staff who stopped apologizing to patients for waiting on the system.

I also mentor three junior developers on the team. I watch them make mistakes I recognize. Occasionally I say nothing and let them find the problem themselves. This is harder than it sounds when you can see the bug from three tabs away. Watching them grow is one of the better parts of this job. It reminds me of something I cannot always name.

In healthcare, clarity saves time. Time helps people.
Everything Else

My mother never used a recipe for domoda. She did not need one. She made it the way people make things they have made a thousand times; by feel, by smell, by a kind of knowledge that lives in the hands and not in the head.

I have been trying to reconstruct it in Berlin for ten years. It is a peanut butter stew, Gambian, and it is still not quite right. My German friends are polite about it. That is how I know it is not right. But it is close enough that when I smell it on the stove, I am briefly somewhere else entirely.

Football is still there. I cannot play the way I once played; the knee made that decision for me; but I still watch, still follow, still think about games in the shower the next morning. I play when I can. Some things you do not stop doing; they just change shape.

My friends sometimes catch me smiling at nothing. They ask what I am thinking about. Sometimes I tell them. Sometimes I genuinely do not know. There is a kind of happiness that does not have a reason; it is just there, underneath everything, surfacing without being called. I am not going to explain it. I am just glad it shows up.

I go to the gym. The discipline of showing up when you do not want to, lifting what felt impossible until it does not; I recognize something familiar in it. The gym does not care about your childhood or your pull requests. I find that restful.

I take photographs. Not professionally. Berlin rewards attention if you are willing to slow down for it. I walk around with a camera sometimes; old buildings, doors, the way afternoon light falls differently on the streets in the eastern parts of the city. It is the one thing I do that has no metric attached to it. No deployment, no performance target. Just whether you noticed something worth keeping.

I still get genuinely excited by cloud infrastructure. AWS, containers, serverless setups; not because they are fashionable, but because they are the infrastructure underneath everything. How things scale. How they stay up when they should. That interest never left.
These things; the football, the domoda, the gym, the smiling for no reason; they are not separate from the work. They are the same person.

I am grateful for the people along the way. My family in The Gambia. My teammates on the pitch. The colleagues in every room I have worked in. The children in that first classroom. The doctor who stopped keeping a paper backup list. The child who saw themselves in a ZULA story for the first time. I still call home.

My mother passed away on June 7th, 2022. The day after my birthday. I had been there with her in The Gambia from December through March, and she was gone three months later. I still have her voice notes on my phone. I play them sometimes. Once to hear what she was saying. Once just to hear her voice.

privacyMeta.subtitle: How this portfolio site handles personal data when you browse, submit a form, or choose optional analytics.

privacySections.title: Who is responsible
privacySections.content:
- This website is operated by **Ansumana Darboe (Ansu)**, a software engineer based in Berlin, Germany. I am the data controller for personal data processed through this site.
- Questions about this notice or your data: [thisisansumana@gmail.com](mailto:thisisansumana@gmail.com).
- This page explains my practices in plain language. It is **not legal advice**. If you need formal legal guidance, speak with a qualified professional.

privacySections.title: What data is involved
privacySections.content:
- I collect only what is needed to run the site and respond to you. I do **not** sell personal data or run advertising profiles.
- **Forms:** contact and project enquiries (name, email, message; project requests may also include website URL, budget range, and timeline). Testimonial feedback (message; name, email, and role only if you choose not to submit anonymously).
- **Technical data:** when you visit, [Netlify](https://www.netlify.com/privacy/) and similar infrastructure may process connection data such as IP address, timestamp, requested URL, browser type, and referrer. This is typical web hosting telemetry used to deliver pages and keep the site reliable.
- **Optional analytics:** if you accept analytics, Google Analytics may receive page views and related usage signals. IP anonymisation is enabled in the configuration I use.
- **Local preferences:** your theme (light/dark) and text size choices are stored in your browser (`localStorage`) so the site remembers your settings. Your analytics choice (accept or decline) is also stored locally.
- **Spotlight assistant:** questions you type in the on-site Spotlight chat are matched against content bundled with this site. Processing happens in your browser session; messages are **not** sent to an external AI API or stored on my server.
- I do not intentionally collect special-category data (for example health information) through this website. Please avoid sending sensitive details in form messages unless they are genuinely needed.

privacySections.title: Why data is processed
privacySections.content:
- To read and reply to messages you send through the forms.
- To operate, secure, and maintain the website (hosting, abuse prevention, troubleshooting).
- To understand aggregate traffic patterns when you have opted in to analytics, so I can improve content and performance.
- To remember accessibility-related display preferences you set.
- To meet legal obligations where they apply.
- I do not use automated decision-making or profiling that produces legal or similarly significant effects.

privacySections.title: Legal bases (GDPR)
privacySections.content:
- **Form submissions:** Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR when processing is necessary to respond to your request or take steps before a potential engagement; otherwise Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in handling professional enquiries directed at me).
- **Hosting and security logs:** Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in running a secure, available website).
- **Optional analytics:** Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR (your consent). Analytics scripts load only after you accept; declining means they are not loaded.
- **Display preferences in localStorage:** Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in providing a usable, accessible experience), or your consent where required for non-essential storage.
- You can withdraw analytics consent at any time by declining in the site banner (when shown), clearing site data in your browser, or emailing me. Withdrawal does not affect processing that was lawful before withdrawal.

privacySections.title: Cookies and local storage
privacySections.content:
- This site is intentionally light on tracking. There are **no advertising cookies**.
- **Strictly functional storage:** theme and font-size settings, plus your saved analytics choice, use browser `localStorage`.
- **Analytics:** Google Analytics is used only after consent. Until then, no Google Analytics scripts are loaded. Google may set cookies or similar identifiers if you accept; see [Google's privacy documentation](https://policies.google.com/privacy) for how they handle data.
- **Fonts:** typography is loaded from Google Fonts. When your browser requests those files, Google may receive technical data such as your IP address.
- You can control cookies and local storage through your browser settings. Blocking storage may reset theme preferences or prompt the analytics choice again.

privacySections.title: Hosting and third parties
privacySections.content:
- [Netlify](https://www.netlify.com/privacy/) hosts this site and processes form submissions through Netlify Forms on my behalf.
- **Google** provides optional Analytics (if you consent) and web fonts. [Google's policies](https://policies.google.com/privacy) apply to data they process as an independent provider.
- **Calendly**, **LinkedIn**, **GitHub**, and **Instagram** are linked for scheduling or social profiles. When you follow those links, you leave this site and their terms and privacy policies apply.
- Some providers are based outside the European Economic Area (including the United States). Where required, transfers rely on appropriate safeguards such as the EU Standard Contractual Clauses or equivalent mechanisms offered by the provider. You can request more detail about transfers by email.

privacySections.title: How long data is kept
privacySections.content:
- **Form submissions:** kept only as long as needed to handle your message and any reasonable follow-up, then deleted or archived unless a longer period is required by law (for example tax or legal claims).
- **Hosting logs:** retained according to Netlify's operational schedules, typically for a limited period suited to security and diagnostics.
- **Analytics:** retention follows the settings configured in Google Analytics (commonly months, not indefinite).
- **Local preferences:** consent and display values remain in your browser until you clear them.

privacySections.title: Your rights
privacySections.content:
- If EU/EEA data protection law applies, you may have the right to **access**, **rectify**, **erase**, **restrict**, or **object** to processing, and to **data portability** where applicable.
- If processing is based on consent, you can **withdraw consent** at any time.
- You may lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. In Berlin, the competent authority is the [Berliner Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit](https://www.datenschutz-berlin.de/).
- To exercise your rights, email [thisisansumana@gmail.com](mailto:thisisansumana@gmail.com) with enough detail for me to locate your request. I aim to respond within **one month**, as required by the GDPR.

privacySections.title: Security
privacySections.content:
- The site is served over **HTTPS**. I rely on established hosting and form providers and keep dependencies reasonably up to date.
- No method of transmission or storage is perfectly secure. Please do **not** send passwords, payment card numbers, or highly sensitive information through the contact forms.
- If you believe data shared with me has been compromised, contact me promptly so we can review next steps.

privacySections.title: Changes to this notice

- I may update this notice when the site, tools, or legal requirements change.
- The **"last updated"** date at the top shows the latest revision.
- Material changes will be reflected here; continued use after an update means you should review the new version.
